cell-biology:
**The cell is the basic unit of life, and every cell is built from a small set of biomolecules — this topic covers what cells are made of and how they are organized.**

## Overview
Every organism is made of one or more cells, and all life shares the same chemical toolkit: water, and four classes of biomolecule (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids). This topic asks you to know the parts of a cell, tell cell types apart, and understand proteins (especially enzymes) and $\mathrm{ATP}$. On the EJU it appears as the **first questions** (問1–問2), usually a $+/-$ organelle table or a statement/labeling item about $\mathrm{ATP}$ or protein structure.

## Key concepts
- **Cells** come in two grand types: **prokaryotes** (bacteria; no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles, DNA is a naked circular loop) and **eukaryotes** (nucleus + organelles). Plant and animal cells are both eukaryotic but differ.
- **Organelles** divide labor: the **nucleus** stores DNA, **mitochondria** make $\mathrm{ATP}$ by respiration, **chloroplasts** do photosynthesis (plants only), **ribosomes** build proteins.
- **Biomolecules**: proteins are chains of **amino acids** and do most of the work (enzymes, structure, transport); nucleic acids ($\mathrm{DNA}$/$\mathrm{RNA}$) carry information; carbohydrates and lipids store energy and build membranes.
- **Enzymes** are protein catalysts that speed up the cell's reactions. **ATP** is the universal energy currency linking energy-releasing and energy-using processes.

## Formulas & key facts
- There are exactly **20** kinds of amino acid used to build proteins.
- Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their **own DNA** (endosymbiotic origin) — a favorite EJU fact.
- The cell membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer**, selectively permeable.

## How the EJU tests it
The two openers are a **combination-table** item (a $+/-$ table for structures across prokaryote / animal / plant cells — you assign $A,B,C$ to chloroplast, cell wall, mitochondria) and a **true/false statement** set on an organelle, ATP labeling, or protein-structure levels. Watch for "choose the incorrect statement" phrasing.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing **cell wall** (plants, bacteria) with **cell membrane** (all cells).
- Forgetting prokaryotes still have **ribosomes** and a cell membrane — they only lack the nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
cell-structure:
**A cell's organelles each do one job; knowing which structures a prokaryote, animal cell, and plant cell have is the single most tested cell-biology skill on the EJU.**

## Overview
A cell is not a bag of chemicals but an organized factory. Membrane-bound compartments called **organelles** each carry out specific tasks. The exam's very first question is almost always a table marking which structures are present ($+$) or absent ($-$) in **prokaryotic (原核細胞)**, **animal**, and **plant** cells, so you must memorize the differences cold.

## Key concepts
- **Prokaryote (原核細胞)** vs **eukaryote (真核細胞)**: prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria) have **no nucleus** — their DNA is a circular loop free in the cytoplasm — and no membrane-bound organelles. They DO have a **cell membrane**, **ribosomes**, and usually a **cell wall**. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a true **nucleus** and organelles.
- **Nucleus (核)**: bounded by a double membrane (nuclear envelope) with pores; contains DNA + nucleolus; controls the cell.
- **Mitochondria (ミトコンドリア)**: site of aerobic respiration; double membrane, inner membrane folded into cristae; makes most $\mathrm{ATP}$. Has its own DNA.
- **Chloroplast (葉緑体)**: photosynthesis; contains chlorophyll on stacked **thylakoid** membranes surrounded by **stroma**. Plants and algae only. Has its own DNA.
- **Ribosome (リボソーム)**: tiny granule (not membrane-bound) that synthesizes proteins; found in ALL cells including prokaryotes.
- **Cell membrane (細胞膜)**: phospholipid bilayer, selectively permeable; in every cell.
- **Cell wall (細胞壁)**: rigid outer layer for support; **plants** (cellulose) and **bacteria** have one, **animal cells do not**.
- Other eukaryote organelles: endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi (make/ship proteins), lysosome (digestion, animals), **large central vacuole** (plants).

## Formulas & key facts
- Structures in **all three** cell types: cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosome, DNA.
- **Plant-only** among the big three: cell wall, chloroplast, large vacuole.
- **Animal + plant (not prokaryote)**: nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi.

## How the EJU tests it
A $+/-$ table lists 3 cell columns; you match letters $A,B,C$ to organelles like **chloroplast, cell wall, mitochondria** by reading which cells have them (e.g. a structure present only in the plant column = chloroplast or cell wall). Or a single true/false statement about the ribosome or chloroplast.

## Worked example
A table shows structure $A$ present in plant only, $B$ present in plant + animal but not prokaryote, $C$ present in all three. Then $A=$ chloroplast (or cell wall), $B=$ mitochondria (or nucleus), $C=$ ribosome (or cell membrane). Use a uniquely-plant clue to pin $A$ first.

## Common mistakes
- Saying prokaryotes have **no ribosomes** — false; they translate proteins too.
- Confusing **cell wall** with **cell membrane**; animal cells have the membrane but no wall.
- Forgetting that both mitochondria AND chloroplasts carry their own DNA.
biomolecules-proteins:
**Proteins are amino-acid chains whose folded shape (four structure levels) determines their function; ATP is the cell's energy currency — both are staple opener questions.**

## Overview
Proteins do almost everything in a cell: they are enzymes, structural fibers, transporters, and receptors. A protein's job depends entirely on its 3-D shape, which is built up in levels from its amino-acid sequence. The EJU tests protein **structure levels**, **denaturation**, and the **structure of $\mathrm{ATP}$** — usually as a true/false statement set or a molecule-labeling item.

## Key concepts
- **Amino acid (アミノ酸)**: the monomer of proteins. There are **20** kinds. Each has an amino group ($\mathrm{-NH_2}$), a carboxyl group ($\mathrm{-COOH}$), and a variable **side chain (R group)** that gives it its properties.
- **Peptide bond**: joins amino acids into a chain (a polypeptide) by linking one's $\mathrm{-COOH}$ to the next's $\mathrm{-NH_2}$, releasing water.
- **Four structure levels**:
  - **Primary structure (一次構造)** = the linear **sequence** of amino acids, set by the gene.
  - **Secondary structure (二次構造)** = local folding held by hydrogen bonds: the **α-helix** (coil) and **β-sheet (β-シート)** (pleated).
  - **Tertiary structure** = the overall 3-D fold of one polypeptide.
  - **Quaternary structure** = several folded chains (subunits) assembled together (e.g. hemoglobin = 4 subunits).
- **Denaturation (変性)**: heat, extreme pH, or chemicals break the weak bonds holding secondary/tertiary structure, so the protein unfolds and **loses function**. The primary sequence (peptide bonds) is NOT broken. Usually irreversible (a cooked egg).
- **Enzyme (酵素)**: a protein catalyst; its active site fits a specific substrate, so it works best at an optimum temperature and pH and stops when denatured.
- **ATP (アデノシン三リン酸)**: **adenine + ribose (= adenosine) + 3 phosphate groups**. Energy is stored in the bonds between phosphates.

## Formulas & key facts
- $$\mathrm{ATP} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{ADP} + P_i + \text{energy}$$
Breaking the terminal phosphate bond ($\mathrm{ATP}\to\mathrm{ADP}$) releases usable energy; respiration/photosynthesis re-attach it.
- **Adenosine** = adenine + ribose (no phosphate). **ADP** = adenosine + 2 phosphates.

## How the EJU tests it
Given an $\mathrm{ATP}$ schematic, choose the combination naming parts $A$–$E$ (ribose, adenine, phosphate, adenosine, ADP). Or a true/false set: "there are 20 amino acids," "the α-helix is secondary structure," "denaturation breaks peptide bonds" (false).

## Worked example
In an ATP diagram, the sugar ring = **ribose**, the double-ring base = **adenine**, ring+sugar together = **adenosine**, the three linked circles = **phosphate** groups. Removing one phosphate gives **ADP**.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking denaturation breaks the **primary structure** — it does not; peptide bonds survive.
- Mislabeling **adenosine** (base+sugar) vs **adenine** (base only).
- Forgetting the count is exactly **20** amino acids.
metabolism:
**Metabolism is the cell's whole set of chemical reactions — breaking molecules down to release energy (respiration) and building them up using energy (photosynthesis, assimilation), with ATP as the shuttle between them.**

## Overview
Life needs a constant supply of usable energy and building materials. **Metabolism** is all the reactions that provide them, split into **catabolism** (break-down, releases energy) and **anabolism** (build-up, uses energy). This topic covers **respiration**, **photosynthesis**, and **nitrogen assimilation/fixation**. On the EJU these are 3–4 items (問3–問4 region): mitochondrion/chloroplast diagrams, assigning reactions to photosystems, and identifying nitrogen-fixing organisms.

## Key concepts
- **Catabolism vs anabolism**: respiration breaks glucose down for energy; photosynthesis and nitrogen assimilation build sugars and amino acids using energy.
- **ATP as the currency**: energy released by respiration is captured as $\mathrm{ATP}$, then spent by anabolic reactions. $\mathrm{ATP}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{ADP}+P_i$.
- **Enzymes** catalyze every step; each reaction has its own enzyme, and pathways run in ordered stages.
- **Electron carriers** ($\mathrm{NADH}$, $\mathrm{NADPH}$, $\mathrm{FADH_2}$) shuttle high-energy electrons between reactions.
- **Assimilation** = building complex substances from simple inorganic ones: carbon assimilation (photosynthesis fixes $\mathrm{CO_2}$) and nitrogen assimilation (builds amino acids from $\mathrm{NH_4^+}/\mathrm{NO_3^-}$).

## Formulas & key facts
- Respiration: $$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O}$$
- Photosynthesis (net): $$\mathrm{6CO_2 + 12H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 + 6H_2O}$$
- Respiration and photosynthesis are near-mirror images but use different pathways and organelles.

## How the EJU tests it
Diagram- and assignment-driven: label parts of a **mitochondrion** (matrix, inner membrane, ATP synthase) or **chloroplast**; assign reactions ($\mathrm{CO_2}$ reduction, water-splitting/$\mathrm{O_2}$ release, light absorption) to **photosystem I / II / Calvin cycle**; pick the correct set of **nitrogen-fixing organisms**.

## Common mistakes
- Saying photosynthesis and respiration are the exact reverse — they share no enzymes and occur in different organelles.
- Mixing up which stage happens where (glycolysis in cytoplasm, not mitochondria).
respiration:
**Aerobic respiration extracts energy from glucose in three stages — glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain — storing it as ATP.**

## Overview
Cells "burn" glucose slowly, capturing the released energy as $\mathrm{ATP}$. Aerobic respiration has **three stages** in specific locations, and the EJU loves to test **where** each stage happens and **what** it produces, usually via a labeled mitochondrion diagram. Oxygen is used only at the very end.

## Key concepts
- **Glycolysis (解糖系)**: in the **cytoplasm** (no membrane, no $\mathrm{O_2}$ needed). One glucose ($\mathrm{C_6}$) is split into **2 pyruvate** ($\mathrm{C_3}$), making a small **net 2 ATP** and 2 $\mathrm{NADH}$.
- **Citric acid cycle (クエン酸回路)** (= Krebs / TCA cycle): in the **matrix (マトリックス)** of the mitochondrion. Pyruvate is fully broken down, releasing $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and loading electron carriers $\mathrm{NADH}$ and $\mathrm{FADH_2}$; a little ATP is made directly.
- **Electron transport chain (電子伝達系)**: on the **inner membrane** of the mitochondrion. $\mathrm{NADH}$ and $\mathrm{FADH_2}$ deliver electrons that pump $\mathrm{H^+}$; the return flow of $\mathrm{H^+}$ through **ATP synthase (ATP合成酵素)** makes the **bulk of the ATP**. $\mathrm{O_2}$ is the **final electron acceptor**, forming $\mathrm{H_2O}$.
- **Anaerobic respiration / fermentation**: without $\mathrm{O_2}$, only glycolysis runs. Yeast → alcoholic fermentation (ethanol + $\mathrm{CO_2}$); muscle → lactic-acid fermentation. Very little ATP.

## Formulas & key facts
- Overall: $$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O}\quad(\approx 38\ \mathrm{ATP})$$
- $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is released in the citric acid cycle (and pyruvate oxidation), NOT in the electron transport chain.
- $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and most ATP are made at the electron transport chain, where $\mathrm{O_2}$ is consumed.

## How the EJU tests it
Using a **mitochondrion diagram**, fill blanks $a$–$c$: the electron transport chain sits on the **inner membrane**, protein complexes pump $\mathrm{H^+}$, $\mathrm{ATP}$ synthase makes ATP; or label the **three stages $A$–$D$** and assign their inputs/outputs ($\mathrm{O_2}$ in, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ out, pyruvate). Watch for "where is the most ATP made?" (inner membrane).

## Worked example
"Which stage occurs in the matrix and releases $\mathrm{CO_2}$?" → the **citric acid cycle**. "Where is $\mathrm{O_2}$ used?" → the **electron transport chain** (inner membrane), as the final electron acceptor.

## Common mistakes
- Placing **glycolysis** in the mitochondrion — it is in the **cytoplasm**.
- Thinking $\mathrm{O_2}$ is used throughout — it acts only at the **end** (electron transport chain).
- Confusing where $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is released (cycle, not transport chain).
photosynthesis:
**Photosynthesis captures light energy (photosystems II and I on the thylakoid) to make ATP and NADPH, then uses them to fix CO2 into sugar (Calvin–Benson cycle in the stroma).**

## Overview
Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria build sugar from $\mathrm{CO_2}$ using light. The process has a **light-dependent stage** on the thylakoid membranes and a **carbon-fixing stage** in the stroma. The EJU's signature item assigns three reactions — $\mathrm{CO_2}$ reduction, water-splitting/$\mathrm{O_2}$ release, light absorption — to **photosystem II, photosystem I, and the Calvin–Benson cycle**.

## Key concepts
- **Chloroplast layout**: stacked **thylakoid (チラコイド)** membranes (light reactions) bathed in fluid **stroma (ストロマ)** (Calvin cycle).
- **Photosystem II (光化学系II)**: absorbs light and **splits water** ($\mathrm{H_2O}$), releasing $\mathrm{O_2}$ and providing electrons and $\mathrm{H^+}$. The $\mathrm{O_2}$ we breathe comes from **water**, not $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
- **Photosystem I (光化学系I)**: absorbs light and passes electrons to reduce $\mathrm{NADP^+}$ to **NADPH**. Electron flow between the photosystems also drives $\mathrm{ATP}$ synthesis.
- **Calvin–Benson cycle (カルビン・ベンソン回路)**: in the **stroma**; uses the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to **reduce (fix) $\mathrm{CO_2}$** into sugar. It needs no light directly but depends on the light reactions' products.
- **Special photosynthesis**: **cyanobacteria (シアノバクテリア)** are prokaryotes that do plant-type (oxygen-releasing) photosynthesis without chloroplasts. **Green/purple sulfur bacteria** use **bacteriochlorophyll** and $\mathrm{H_2S}$ instead of water, releasing **sulfur, not $\mathrm{O_2}$**.

## Formulas & key facts
- Overall: $$\mathrm{6CO_2 + 12H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 + 6H_2O}$$
- Released $\mathrm{O_2}$ originates from **water** (isotope-labeling evidence).
- Light reactions make **ATP + NADPH**; the Calvin cycle consumes them.

## How the EJU tests it
Assign reactions $a$ ($\mathrm{CO_2}$ reduction), $b$ (water electron donation + $\mathrm{O_2}$ release), $c$ (light absorption) across **photosystem I, photosystem II, Calvin–Benson cycle**. Or true/false on green-sulfur-bacteria or cyanobacterial carbon assimilation. Know that water-splitting = photosystem II; $\mathrm{CO_2}$ reduction = Calvin cycle.

## Worked example
"Which process releases $\mathrm{O_2}$?" → water-splitting at **photosystem II**. "Which fixes $\mathrm{CO_2}$?" → the **Calvin–Benson cycle** in the stroma. "Which uses bacteriochlorophyll and does not release $\mathrm{O_2}$?" → green sulfur bacteria.

## Common mistakes
- Saying the released $\mathrm{O_2}$ comes from $\mathrm{CO_2}$ — it comes from **water**.
- Calling the Calvin cycle "dark reactions" and thinking it works without the light stage's ATP/NADPH.
- Assuming all photosynthetic bacteria release $\mathrm{O_2}$ (sulfur bacteria do not).
nitrogen-metabolism:
**Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2 into ammonium (only certain bacteria can do it), while nitrogen assimilation builds amino acids and nucleic acids from absorbed nitrogen.**

## Overview
Organisms need nitrogen for proteins and nucleic acids, but plants and animals cannot use the abundant $\mathrm{N_2}$ gas directly. Two distinct processes matter: **nitrogen fixation** (turning $\mathrm{N_2}$ into a usable form, done only by special microbes) and **nitrogen assimilation** (plants building organic molecules from absorbed nitrogen). The EJU tests these mainly by asking you to **identify the correct set of nitrogen-fixing organisms**.

## Key concepts
- **Nitrogen fixation (窒素固定)**: reduction of atmospheric $\mathrm{N_2}$ to ammonium $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$. Only certain **prokaryotes** can do it:
  - **Root nodule bacteria (根粒菌, Rhizobium)** — live symbiotically in legume root nodules.
  - **Azotobacter** and **Clostridium** — free-living soil bacteria (aerobic and anaerobic respectively).
  - **Nostoc (ネンジュモ)** and other cyanobacteria.
- **Nitrogen assimilation (窒素同化)**: plants absorb nitrogen as **nitrate $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$** or **ammonium $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$** from soil, then build **amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids**. (Assimilation ≠ fixation.)
- **Nitrifying bacteria (硝化菌)**: soil bacteria that oxidize $\mathrm{NH_4^+}\to\mathrm{NO_2^-}\to\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ (**nitrification**); this makes nitrate available to plants but is NOT nitrogen fixation.
- **Denitrifying bacteria**: return nitrogen to the air as $\mathrm{N_2}$ (denitrification).

## Formulas & key facts
- Fixation: $\mathrm{N_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_4^+}$ (only special bacteria).
- Nitrification: $\mathrm{NH_4^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_3^-}$.
- Legumes enrich soil because their root-nodule bacteria fix nitrogen.

## How the EJU tests it
"Choose the correct set of **nitrogen-fixing organisms**" — the right answer includes Nostoc, Clostridium, Azotobacter, and root-nodule bacteria, but **excludes** nitrifying bacteria and ordinary plants. Or a blank-fill distinguishing **assimilation** (building organic molecules) from **fixation** ($\mathrm{N_2}\to\mathrm{NH_4^+}$) and naming the role of root-nodule bacteria.

## Worked example
"Which can fix atmospheric nitrogen: (i) Rhizobium, (ii) nitrifying bacteria, (iii) Azotobacter, (iv) Nostoc?" → **i, iii, iv**. Nitrifying bacteria only convert $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ to nitrate; they cannot fix $\mathrm{N_2}$.

## Common mistakes
- Calling **nitrifying bacteria** nitrogen fixers — they are not; they oxidize ammonium to nitrate.
- Confusing **assimilation** (organic-molecule building) with **fixation** ($\mathrm{N_2}$ reduction).
- Thinking plants can use $\mathrm{N_2}$ gas directly — they need $\mathrm{NH_4^+}/\mathrm{NO_3^-}$.
genetics-molecular:
**Genes are DNA sequences that are copied, expressed into proteins, and passed on — this topic spans DNA replication, transcription/translation, genetic engineering, inheritance, and mutation.**

## Overview
DNA stores hereditary information; the **central dogma** is $\mathrm{DNA}\to\mathrm{RNA}\to\text{protein}$. This topic covers how DNA is **copied** (replication), **read out** into proteins (transcription, splicing, translation), **manipulated** in the lab (PCR, gene transfer), **inherited** (Mendelian genetics, linkage), and **changed** (mutation). It is one of the largest EJU blocks (問5–問9 region), including the exam's few short calculations.

## Key concepts
- **DNA structure**: a double helix of two complementary strands; bases pair **A–T** and **G–C** by hydrogen bonds. Replication is **semi-conservative**.
- **Gene expression**: **transcription** makes mRNA in the nucleus; **splicing** removes introns; **translation** at ribosomes reads mRNA in three-base **codons** to build a protein.
- **The genetic code** is a triplet code, redundant, and nearly universal.
- **Genetic engineering**: **PCR** amplifies DNA; **plasmids** carry genes into bacteria; **restriction enzymes** and **DNA ligase** cut and join DNA.
- **Inheritance**: alleles segregate (Mendel's ratios); linked genes are inherited together unless **crossing over** recombines them.
- **Mutation**: changes in the DNA sequence (e.g. base substitution) that can alter a protein.

## Formulas & key facts
- Chargaff: $\%\mathrm{A}=\%\mathrm{T}$, $\%\mathrm{G}=\%\mathrm{C}$.
- PCR doubles DNA each cycle: $2^n$ copies after $n$ cycles.
- Recombination frequency $=\dfrac{\text{recombinant offspring}}{\text{total offspring}}\times100\%$.

## How the EJU tests it
Mechanism blank-fills (name enzymes, $5'\to3'$ direction, exon/intron splicing), a **genetic-code deduction** from synthetic-mRNA data, a **PCR/insulin gene-transfer** labeling item, and light **linkage calculations** (recombination frequency, segregation ratio).

## Common mistakes
- Swapping **transcription** (→ RNA, nucleus) and **translation** (→ protein, ribosome).
- Forgetting RNA uses **U** instead of T.
dna-replication:
**DNA is an antiparallel double helix that copies itself semi-conservatively: helicase unzips it, and DNA polymerase builds each new strand 5'→3' on a template.**

## Overview
DNA must be copied exactly before a cell divides. Its structure — two complementary strands wound into a **double helix (二重らせん)** — is what makes accurate copying possible: each old strand serves as a **template (鋳型)** for a new one. The EJU tests the **enzymes**, the **base-pairing rules**, and the **$5'\to3'$ direction** of synthesis.

## Key concepts
- **Double helix**: two strands of nucleotides (sugar–phosphate backbone + base) twisted together. The strands are **antiparallel** (one runs $5'\to3'$, the other $3'\to5'$).
- **Base pairing**: **A pairs with T** (2 hydrogen bonds), **G pairs with C** (3 hydrogen bonds). Pairing is **complementary**, so one strand's sequence dictates the other's.
- **DNA helicase (DNAヘリカーゼ)**: unwinds the helix by breaking the **hydrogen bonds** between paired bases, separating the two strands.
- **DNA polymerase (DNAポリメラーゼ)**: reads each template strand and adds complementary nucleotides, always synthesizing the new strand in the **$5'\to3'$ direction**.
- **Semi-conservative replication**: each new double helix has **one old (template) strand + one new strand** (Meselson–Stahl experiment).
- **Leading vs lagging strand**: because synthesis is only $5'\to3'$, one new strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in short **Okazaki fragments** (lagging), later joined by **DNA ligase**.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Chargaff's rule**: $\%\mathrm{A}=\%\mathrm{T}$ and $\%\mathrm{G}=\%\mathrm{C}$; also $\%\mathrm{A}+\%\mathrm{G}+\%\mathrm{T}+\%\mathrm{C}=100\%$. Knowing one fraction gives the rest.
- New strands always grow **$5'\to3'$**; the template is read $3'\to5'$.
- Number of hydrogen bonds: A–T = 2, G–C = 3.

## How the EJU tests it
Fill blanks $a$–$c$: **helicase** breaks hydrogen bonds, **polymerase** copies each template, the new strand grows **$5'\to3'$**. Or choose the correct **replication-direction diagram** (which arrows show valid $5'\to3'$ synthesis). Or a base-count calculation using Chargaff's rule.

## Worked example
If a DNA molecule is $30\%$ A, then T $=30\%$, so A+T $=60\%$, leaving G+C $=40\%$, hence G $=20\%$ and C $=20\%$.

## Common mistakes
- Pairing A with C or G — A always pairs with **T**.
- Thinking DNA polymerase can build $3'\to5'$ — it only works **$5'\to3'$**.
- Confusing semi-conservative with conservative (each new helix keeps **one** old strand).
transcription-translation:
**Gene expression flows DNA→mRNA→protein: RNA polymerase transcribes from a promoter, splicing removes introns, and ribosomes translate codons into amino acids using tRNA anticodons.**

## Overview
A gene's instructions become a protein in stages. **Transcription** copies DNA into messenger RNA; in eukaryotes **splicing** trims the RNA; **translation** reads it three bases at a time to assemble a protein. The EJU tests the enzymes and sites, the exon/intron logic of **splicing**, and reading a **codon table** — including deducing codons from experimental data.

## Key concepts
- **Transcription (転写)**: **RNA polymerase (RNAポリメラーゼ)** binds a **promoter (プロモーター)** on the DNA and copies one (template) strand into **mRNA (mRNA)**. RNA uses **uracil (U)** in place of thymine (T).
- **Splicing (スプライシング)**: the first RNA (pre-mRNA) contains coding **exons (エキソン)** interrupted by non-coding **introns (イントロン)**. Splicing **cuts out introns and joins exons** to make mature mRNA that leaves the nucleus.
- **Translation (翻訳)**: at the **ribosome**, mRNA is read in **codons (コドン)** — groups of **3 bases = 1 amino acid**. **tRNA** carries an amino acid and has an **anticodon (アンチコドン)** complementary to the codon.
- **The genetic code (遺伝暗号)**: a triplet code. **Start codon** = $\mathrm{AUG}$ (methionine); **stop codons** ($\mathrm{UAA}$, $\mathrm{UAG}$, $\mathrm{UGA}$) end translation. The code is **redundant** (several codons per amino acid) and nearly **universal**.

## Formulas & key facts
- **3 bases → 1 amino acid**, so a coding region of $n$ codons = $3n$ bases → $n$ amino acids (minus the stop).
- DNA template $\to$ mRNA: complementary, with A→U (template A gives mRNA U), and read the **codon table on the mRNA**.
- $4^3 = 64$ possible codons encode 20 amino acids + stop signals (hence redundancy).

## How the EJU tests it
Blank-fills on transcription (RNA polymerase + promoter) and splicing (introns removed, exons joined). A classic **code-deduction** item: from repeated synthetic mRNAs (e.g. $\mathrm{UGUGUG\ldots}$, $\mathrm{UUGUUG\ldots}$, $\mathrm{GGUGGU\ldots}$) and the resulting polypeptides, deduce the codon for a given amino acid.

## Worked example
mRNA $\mathrm{GGUGGU\ldots}$ gives a polypeptide of only glycine, so a glycine codon is $\mathrm{GGU}$. mRNA $\mathrm{UGUGUG\ldots}$ read in frames gives alternating $\mathrm{UGU}$/$\mathrm{GUG}$ → two amino acids; cross-referencing with another repeat pins the codon for cysteine as $\mathrm{UGU}$.

## Common mistakes
- Reading the codon table off the **DNA** instead of the **mRNA**.
- Forgetting **U replaces T** in RNA.
- Swapping **exon** (expressed, kept) and **intron** (removed).
genetic-engineering:
**Genetic engineering moves genes between organisms using plasmid vectors and DNA ligase, while PCR rapidly amplifies a DNA region by repeated heat cycling with primers and DNA polymerase.**

## Overview
Biotechnology lets us copy and transfer genes. **PCR** makes millions of copies of a chosen DNA region in a test tube; **gene transfer** inserts a gene (e.g. the human insulin gene) into bacteria so they mass-produce a protein. The EJU tests the **PCR cycle steps** and a **gene-transfer labeling** scheme (plasmid, gene, host).

## Key concepts
- **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)**: amplifies DNA through repeated temperature cycles:
  1. **Denature** (~$95^\circ\mathrm{C}$): heat breaks the **hydrogen bonds**, separating the two DNA strands.
  2. **Anneal** (~$55^\circ\mathrm{C}$): short **primers (プライマー)** bind to the target ends (a primer marks where copying starts).
  3. **Extend** (~$72^\circ\mathrm{C}$): heat-stable **DNA polymerase** builds new strands from the primers.
- Each cycle **doubles** the DNA, so $n$ cycles give $2^n$ copies.
- **Plasmid (プラスミド)**: a small circular DNA in bacteria used as a **vector** to carry a gene into a host.
- **Restriction enzymes** cut DNA at specific sequences; **DNA ligase (DNAリガーゼ)** joins the cut gene into the plasmid, making **recombinant (遺伝子組換え) DNA**.
- **Host / delivery**: the recombinant plasmid is taken up by **E. coli (大腸菌)**, which then expresses the gene (e.g. produces human insulin). For plants, **Agrobacterium** transfers genes into plant cells.

## Formulas & key facts
- After $n$ PCR cycles: number of copies $\approx 2^n$ (e.g. $2^{10}=1024$-fold in 10 cycles).
- DNA is **negatively charged**, so in gel electrophoresis it migrates toward the **positive** electrode; **shorter fragments move faster/farther**.

## How the EJU tests it
Label $A,B,C$ in an **insulin-production scheme**: the **human insulin gene** is cut out, inserted with **DNA ligase** into a **plasmid**, which enters **E. coli**. Or fill **PCR-principle** blanks: hydrogen bonds break on heating, **primers** bind, **DNA polymerase** extends; each cycle doubles the copies.

## Worked example
In a gene-transfer diagram, $A$ = human insulin gene (cut from human DNA), $B$ = plasmid (vector), $C$ = E. coli (host that mass-produces insulin). Ligase joins $A$ into $B$; $B$ enters $C$.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing the **primer** (short starter that DNA polymerase extends) with the whole new strand.
- Forgetting PCR uses a **heat-stable** polymerase (survives the $95^\circ\mathrm{C}$ step).
- Mixing up **ligase** (joins) and **restriction enzyme** (cuts).
mendelian-linkage:
**Alleles segregate to give Mendelian ratios, but genes on the same chromosome are linked and inherited together unless crossing over recombines them — recombination frequency measures how often this happens.**

## Overview
Inheritance follows rules. A single gene gives Mendel's $3{:}1$ and $1{:}1$ ratios; two genes on different chromosomes give $9{:}3{:}3{:}1$. But genes on the **same** chromosome are **linked** and travel together, distorting these ratios; **crossing over** shuffles them, producing recombinants. The EJU's few calculations live here: **recombination frequency** and **segregation ratios**.

## Key concepts
- **Allele (対立遺伝子)**: alternative versions of a gene; **dominant** (capital, e.g. $A$) masks **recessive** ($a$). **Genotype (遺伝子型)** = allele pair; **phenotype** = the visible trait.
- **Segregation**: alleles separate into gametes. $Aa\times Aa \to$ **3 dominant : 1 recessive** ($1{:}2{:}1$ genotype). **Test cross** ($\times aa$) reveals a genotype: $Aa\times aa \to 1{:}1$.
- **Independent assortment** (genes on different chromosomes): dihybrid $AaBb\times AaBb \to 9{:}3{:}3{:}1$.
- **Linkage (連鎖)**: genes on the **same chromosome** are inherited together, so parental combinations dominate and the $9{:}3{:}3{:}1$ ratio breaks down.
- **Crossing over (乗換え)**: homologous chromosomes exchange segments during meiosis I, creating **recombinant** gametes. The closer two genes, the rarer the crossover.
- **Recombination frequency (組換え価)**: percentage of recombinant offspring; it is proportional to the **map distance** between genes, so it builds a **gene map (染色体地図)**.

## Formulas & key facts
- $$\text{Recombination frequency} = \frac{\text{number of recombinant offspring}}{\text{total offspring}}\times 100\%$$
- From a **test cross**, offspring phenotypes directly reveal the gamete ratio. Parental (non-recombinant) types are the majority; recombinant types are the minority (except at $50\%$, = unlinked).
- Map distance (in units) $\approx$ recombination frequency ($\%$).

## How the EJU tests it
From a test-cross ratio like $[AB]{:}[Ab]{:}[aB]{:}[ab]=8{:}1{:}1{:}8$, compute the **percentage of recombinant gametes**. Or determine new gamete genotypes and the **timing of crossing over** (meiosis I). Or read a self-cross ratio distorted by linkage.

## Worked example
Test cross gives $[AB]{:}[Ab]{:}[aB]{:}[ab]=8{:}1{:}1{:}8$ (total $=18$). Parentals are $AB$ and $ab$ ($8+8=16$); recombinants are $Ab$ and $aB$ ($1+1=2$). Recombination frequency $=\dfrac{2}{18}\times100\%\approx 11\%$.

## Common mistakes
- Treating linked genes as if independent ($9{:}3{:}3{:}1$) — linkage makes parentals dominate.
- Mixing up which classes are **recombinant** (the minority, non-parental combinations).
- Forgetting a test cross uses the **homozygous recessive** parent.
mutation:
**A gene mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence; a single base substitution can change one amino acid, as in sickle-cell anemia.**

## Overview
Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence — the ultimate source of genetic variation and the raw material of evolution. The EJU focuses on **point mutations**, especially **base substitution**, and the classic example of **sickle-cell anemia**, often asking you to deduce a codon from a codon table.

## Key concepts
- **Gene (point) mutation (突然変異)**: a change affecting one or a few bases. Types: **substitution (塩基置換)** (one base swapped), insertion, or deletion.
- **Effects of a substitution** (using the redundant code):
  - **Silent**: the new codon still codes the same amino acid (no change) — possible because the code is redundant.
  - **Missense**: the codon now codes a **different amino acid** → altered protein.
  - **Nonsense**: the codon becomes a **stop codon** → truncated protein.
- **Insertion/deletion** of a number of bases not divisible by 3 causes a **frameshift**, misreading every codon downstream (usually severe).
- **Sickle-cell anemia (鎌状赤血球症)**: a single **base substitution** in the β-hemoglobin gene changes one amino acid (glutamic acid → valine). This one change makes red blood cells sickle-shaped — a textbook example of how a point mutation alters a protein and phenotype.
- Mutations may be neutral, harmful, or (rarely) beneficial; mutagens (UV, chemicals) raise the rate.

## Formulas & key facts
- Because the code is **redundant**, not every base change alters the protein (silent mutations exist).
- A frameshift (indel $\neq$ multiple of 3) is generally more damaging than a single substitution.
- Sickle-cell = **one base substitution → one amino acid change** (Glu → Val).

## How the EJU tests it
Given a **codon table** and the mutant amino acid/codon, deduce the **original codon** (as in the sickle-cell case). Or classify a mutation from before/after sequences and predict its effect on the protein.

## Worked example
Normal hemoglobin has glutamic acid (codon e.g. $\mathrm{GAG}$); the sickle form has valine ($\mathrm{GUG}$). A single $\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{U}$ substitution (second base) converts $\mathrm{GAG}\to\mathrm{GUG}$ — one base changes one amino acid.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming every base change alters the protein — **silent** mutations do not.
- Confusing a **substitution** (one base swapped, no frameshift) with an **insertion/deletion** (can frameshift).
- Reading the codon table off the DNA instead of the mRNA.
reproduction-development:
**Sexual reproduction makes gametes by meiosis and unites them at fertilization; the zygote then develops through stages into a full organism — this topic covers meiosis, plant reproduction, and animal development.**

## Overview
New organisms are made by producing **gametes** (via meiosis, which halves the chromosome number) and combining them at **fertilization** (which restores it), then developing the zygote into a body. This topic covers **meiosis/gametogenesis**, **plant double fertilization**, and **animal development**. On the EJU it is 問7–問9 region: meiosis-stage ordering, **linkage/recombination calculations**, ploidy of seed parts, and gastrula germ-layer labeling.

## Key concepts
- **Meiosis** produces four **haploid ($n$)** cells from one **diploid ($2n$)** cell in two divisions, generating variation through crossing over and independent assortment.
- **Fertilization** fuses two gametes to restore the diploid number and mix two parents' genes.
- **Plant double fertilization**: two sperm nuclei fuse — one with the egg ($\to 2n$ embryo), one with the central cell ($\to 3n$ endosperm).
- **Animal development**: zygote → cleavage → blastula → **gastrula** (three germ layers form) → organ formation. Each germ layer makes specific organs.
- The same genome is present in every cell; **differentiation** is about which genes are expressed.

## Formulas & key facts
- Meiosis: $2n \to n$; DNA replicates **once**, cell divides **twice**.
- Ploidy in the angiosperm seed: **embryo $2n$**, **endosperm $3n$**.
- Germ layers: **ectoderm** (skin, nerves), **mesoderm** (muscle, bone, blood), **endoderm** (gut lining, lungs, liver).

## How the EJU tests it
Order meiosis-stage figures and give chromosome counts; identify which figures are haploid; compute **recombination frequency** from a testcross; identify which cells fuse in **double fertilization** and the number of embryo-sac mother cells for $N$ seeds; label gastrula germ layers and cavities.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing meiosis I (separates **homologues**) with meiosis II (separates **sister chromatids**).
- Forgetting endosperm is **$3n$** (two polar nuclei + one sperm).
- Assigning the nervous system to the wrong germ layer (it is **ectoderm**).
meiosis-gametogenesis:
**Meiosis is two successive divisions that halve the chromosome number (2n→n), producing four haploid gametes and generating genetic variation.**

## Overview
Gametes (sperm, eggs, pollen) must carry **half** the chromosome number so fertilization restores the normal amount. **Meiosis** achieves this in two divisions, and along the way it shuffles genes to create variation. The EJU tests the **difference between meiosis I and II**, the **nuclear phase (核相, ploidy)** at each stage, and ordering the stages / counting chromosomes.

## Key concepts
- **Diploid ($2n$)** vs **haploid ($n$)**: body cells are $2n$ (two of each chromosome, one from each parent); gametes are $n$.
- **Nuclear phase (核相)**: the $n$ or $2n$ state of a cell, tracked through the stages.
- **One replication, two divisions**: DNA is copied **once** (before meiosis I), then the cell divides **twice**, giving **four** cells.
- **Meiosis I (減数第一分裂)** = reduction division: **homologous chromosomes** pair and then separate. This is where the chromosome number halves ($2n\to n$) and where **crossing over** occurs (prophase I).
- **Meiosis II (減数第二分裂)**: like mitosis — **sister chromatids** separate. Number stays $n$.
- **Sources of variation**: crossing over + **independent assortment** of homologues.
- **Gametogenesis (配偶子形成)**:
  - Animals: one primary spermatocyte → **4 sperm**; one primary oocyte → **1 egg + polar bodies**.
  - Plants: meiosis in the anther gives **pollen (花粉)** (male); meiosis in the ovule gives the **embryo sac (胚のう)** (female).

## Formulas & key facts
- $2n \xrightarrow{\text{meiosis I}} n \xrightarrow{\text{meiosis II}} n$ (four haploid cells total).
- DNA amount per cell: doubles at replication, then halves at meiosis I and again at meiosis II.
- Chromosome number is halved at **meiosis I** (not II).

## How the EJU tests it
Order the meiosis-stage figures into the correct sequence and give the **chromosome number** at each; or pick which figures show the **haploid ($n$)** state; or state where crossing over happens (meiosis I).

## Worked example
An organism has $2n=4$. After meiosis I each cell has $n=2$ chromosomes (each still two chromatids); after meiosis II, each of the four cells has $n=2$ single-chromatid chromosomes. So the answer to "chromosome number after meiosis I" is **2**, not 4.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking the number halves at meiosis II — it halves at **meiosis I**.
- Confusing separation of **homologues** (I) with **sister chromatids** (II).
- Forgetting DNA replicates only **once** for the whole of meiosis.
fertilization-plants:
**In flowering plants, double fertilization occurs: one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to form the 2n embryo, and the other fuses with the central cell to form the 3n endosperm.**

## Overview
Flowering plants (angiosperms) have a unique **double fertilization**: two sperm nuclei from one pollen grain are used, producing both the embryo and its food store. The EJU tests the **structure of the embryo sac**, **which cells fuse**, the **ploidy** of the products, and where meiosis occurs.

## Key concepts
- **Pollen tube (花粉管)**: when pollen lands on the stigma, it grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovule, delivering **two sperm nuclei**.
- **Embryo sac (胚のう)** — the female gametophyte inside the ovule — contains **7 cells / 8 nuclei**:
  - **Egg cell (卵細胞)** ($n$) — the female gamete.
  - **Two synergids (助細胞)** flanking the egg.
  - **Central cell (中央細胞)** with **two polar nuclei** ($n+n$).
  - **Three antipodal cells (反足細胞)** at the far end.
- **Double fertilization (重複受精)** — the two fusions:
  - Sperm ($n$) + **egg cell** ($n$) → **zygote → embryo** ($2n$).
  - Sperm ($n$) + **central cell** (two polar nuclei, $n+n$) → **endosperm (胚乳)** ($3n$), the nutrient store.
- **Where meiosis occurs**: the **embryo-sac mother cell (胚のう母細胞)** in the ovule undergoes meiosis to form the embryo sac; similarly pollen forms via meiosis in the anther.
- **After fertilization**: ovule → **seed**, ovary → **fruit**.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Embryo = $2n$**; **endosperm = $3n$** (two polar nuclei + one sperm). Seed coat (from the ovule wall) = $2n$ maternal tissue.
- One embryo-sac mother cell → one embryo sac → potentially one seed, so **$N$ seeds need $N$ mother cells**.
- Only **angiosperms** perform double fertilization.

## How the EJU tests it
From a mature pollen + embryo-sac diagram, identify which two structures fuse to form the **embryo** (egg + sperm) and which form the **endosperm** (central cell + sperm); give the ploidy; state where **meiosis** occurs and the **number of mother cells** needed for $N$ seeds.

## Worked example
"Which fusion makes the endosperm, and what is its ploidy?" → the **central cell** (with two polar nuclei, $n+n$) fuses with one **sperm** ($n$), giving a **$3n$** endosperm.

## Common mistakes
- Saying endosperm is $2n$ — it is **$3n$** (three nuclei fuse).
- Confusing **synergids/antipodal cells** with the egg (only the egg becomes the embryo).
- Thinking gymnosperms do double fertilization — only **angiosperms** do.
animal-development:
**After cleavage the animal embryo forms a hollow blastula, then gastrulates into three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), each giving rise to specific organs.**

## Overview
A fertilized egg becomes a body through ordered stages. Early divisions (cleavage) make a hollow ball, which then folds inward to form the **gastrula** with its three **germ layers**. The EJU tests the **order of stages**, labeling **gastrula** structures, and which **germ layer** makes which organs.

## Key concepts
- **Cleavage**: rapid divisions with no growth → a hollow **blastula**, whose internal cavity is the **blastocoel (胞胚腔)**.
- **Gastrulation** → the **gastrula (原腸胚)**: cells move inward, forming a new gut cavity, the **archenteron (原腸)**, which opens at the blastopore. Three **germ layers (胚葉)** now exist:
  - **Ectoderm (外胚葉)** (outer) → epidermis (skin) and the **nervous system**.
  - **Mesoderm (中胚葉)** (middle) → muscle, bone, blood, heart, kidney, gonads.
  - **Endoderm (内胚葉)** (inner) → lining of the **gut**, and the lungs, liver, pancreas.
- **Blastocoel vs archenteron**: the blastocoel is the blastula's cavity (shrinks during gastrulation); the archenteron is the new gut cavity of the gastrula.
- **Stage order**: fertilized egg → cleavage → **blastula** → **gastrula** → neurula → organ formation.
- **Induction**: one tissue signals a neighbor to differentiate (e.g. the dorsal-lip organizer induces the neural tube) — Spemann's classic experiment.

## Formulas & key facts
- Three germ layers: **ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm** — memorize their organs.
- Nervous system + skin epidermis = **ectoderm**; gut/lung/liver linings = **endoderm**; muscle/bone/blood = **mesoderm**.
- Every cell keeps the **same DNA**; differentiation is differential **gene expression**.

## How the EJU tests it
Label $A$–$C$ in a **gastrula diagram**: identify the **ectoderm/mesoderm/endoderm**, the **blastocoel**, and the **archenteron**; or match an organ to its germ layer; or put the developmental stages in order.

## Worked example
"From which germ layer does the brain develop?" → the **ectoderm** (which also forms the epidermis). "Which cavity is the gut of the gastrula?" → the **archenteron**.

## Common mistakes
- Assigning the nervous system to mesoderm — it is **ectoderm**.
- Confusing the **blastocoel** (blastula cavity) with the **archenteron** (gastrula gut cavity).
- Reversing the stage order (blastula comes **before** gastrula).
homeostasis:
**Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature, blood sugar, water, pH) by negative feedback, run jointly by the nervous and endocrine systems together with the blood, liver, and kidneys.**

## Overview
Cells work only within narrow limits, so the body holds its internal conditions near set points despite external change. This regulation — **homeostasis** — is achieved by **negative feedback**, coordinated by the fast **nervous system** and the slow **endocrine (hormone)** system. This topic covers **circulation/blood**, **kidney/liver**, **endocrine/blood-sugar**, **autonomic/thermoregulation**, and **immunity** — a large EJU block (問10–問13 region), heavy on **diagram and graph interpretation**.

## Key concepts
- **Negative feedback**: a deviation triggers a response that **reverses** it, returning to the set point (e.g. high blood sugar → insulin → sugar falls).
- **Two control systems**: nerves (fast, brief) and hormones (slower, longer-lasting) share the work; both are often **antagonistic** (opposing pairs).
- **Key organs**: **heart/blood** transport materials and $\mathrm{O_2}$; **kidney** filters blood and balances water/ions; **liver** processes nutrients and detoxifies (ammonia → urea); **pancreas** and other glands secrete hormones.
- **Immunity** defends the internal environment against pathogens using specific and non-specific defenses.
- The **hypothalamus** is a master control center (temperature, water balance, endocrine).

## Formulas & key facts
- **Insulin lowers** blood glucose; **glucagon** and **adrenaline** raise it.
- Concentration ratio in the kidney: $\dfrac{\text{urine conc.}}{\text{plasma/primitive-urine conc.}}$ reveals reabsorption.
- Oxygen loading/unloading is read from the **oxygen-dissociation curve**.

## How the EJU tests it
Interpret **diagrams and graphs**: trace blood through a circulatory diagram, read an **oxygen-dissociation curve**, a **kidney concentration table**, a **blood-glucose regulation diagram** (name nerves and hormones), or an **antibody-titer curve** (primary vs secondary response). Mostly "choose the correct/incorrect statement" or combination items.

## Common mistakes
- Reversing insulin/glucagon roles (insulin is the only sugar-**lowering** hormone).
- Confusing negative feedback (stabilizing) with positive feedback.
circulation-blood:
**The heart pumps blood through a double circulation; hemoglobin loads O2 where oxygen is high and unloads it where oxygen (and CO2) conditions favor release — read this from the oxygen-dissociation curve.**

## Overview
The circulatory system moves oxygen, nutrients, and wastes around the body. The EJU tests **tracing blood** through diagrams (which vessel has most $\mathrm{O_2}$, most glucose, least urea), the **heart's structure and pacemaker**, and — the signature graph — the **oxygen-dissociation curve (酸素解離曲線)** of hemoglobin.

## Key concepts
- **Heart (心臓)**: four chambers (2 atria, 2 ventricles) driving **double circulation** — the right side pumps to the **lungs** (pulmonary), the left side to the **body** (systemic). Blood flows atria → ventricles → arteries.
- **Blood vessels (血管)**: **arteries** carry blood **away** from the heart; **veins** carry it **back**. Note: the **pulmonary artery** carries **venous (deoxygenated) blood**, the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood — a favorite trap.
- **Arterial vs venous blood (静脈血)**: arterial = oxygen-rich (bright red); venous = oxygen-poor.
- **Sinoatrial node (洞房結節)**: the heart's **pacemaker** in the right atrium; it sets the heartbeat automatically (modulated by autonomic nerves).
- **Hemoglobin (ヘモグロビン)**: the red-blood-cell protein that binds $\mathrm{O_2}$. Loads $\mathrm{O_2}$ in the lungs (high $\mathrm{O_2}$), releases it in tissues (low $\mathrm{O_2}$, high $\mathrm{CO_2}$).
- **Vessel contents**: after the intestine, the **hepatic portal vein** is richest in glucose; after the kidney, the **renal vein** is lowest in urea/nitrogen waste.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Oxygen-dissociation curve**: S-shaped; the $y$-axis is **% oxyhemoglobin**, $x$-axis is partial pressure of $\mathrm{O_2}$. Higher $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (or higher temperature / lower pH) shifts the curve **right**, so hemoglobin **releases more $\mathrm{O_2}$** in active tissues (Bohr effect).
- % $\mathrm{O_2}$ released to tissue $=$ (oxyhemoglobin % in lungs) $-$ (oxyhemoglobin % in tissue).

## How the EJU tests it
From a circulatory diagram, choose the vessel with (I) **least nitrogenous waste** (renal vein), (II) **most glucose after a meal** (hepatic portal vein), (III) **most oxygen** (pulmonary vein). Or identify venous-blood vessels, the SA-node location, or chamber names. Or read the **oxygen-dissociation curve** to get oxyhemoglobin % at given $\mathrm{O_2}/\mathrm{CO_2}$ conditions.

## Worked example
If hemoglobin is $95\%$ saturated in the lungs and $30\%$ saturated in active muscle, then $95-30=65\%$ of the hemoglobin's oxygen is released to that tissue.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming all **arteries** carry oxygenated blood — the **pulmonary artery** carries deoxygenated blood.
- Reading the dissociation curve backward: a **right shift = more $\mathrm{O_2}$ released**, not more bound.
- Confusing the hepatic portal vein (glucose-rich) with the renal vein (waste-poor).
excretion-liver:
**The kidney's nephron filters blood into primitive urine and then reabsorbs useful substances (glucose, water, ions) to form urine; the liver converts toxic ammonia into urea.**

## Overview
The body must remove nitrogen waste and balance water and ions. The **kidney** does this by **filtering** blood and then **reabsorbing** what the body needs; the **liver** turns toxic ammonia into safer **urea**. The EJU's classic item is a **table of concentrations in primitive urine vs urine** — you deduce which substance is glucose, $\mathrm{Na^+}$, or protein from its filtration/reabsorption behavior.

## Key concepts
- **Nephron** (kidney functional unit): the **glomerulus (糸球体)** is a knot of capillaries that **filters** blood into Bowman's capsule, producing **primitive urine (原尿)**.
- **Filtration**: small molecules (water, glucose, ions, urea) pass into the primitive urine; large molecules like **proteins** and blood cells are **NOT filtered** (too big), so they stay in the blood.
- **Reabsorption (再吸収)**: as primitive urine flows through the tubule, useful substances are returned to the blood. **Glucose is normally 100% reabsorbed** (so none in final urine); much water and $\mathrm{Na^+}$ are reabsorbed; **urea is barely reabsorbed**, so it becomes concentrated in the **urine (尿)**.
- **Deducing components from a table**:
  - **Protein**: present in blood but **absent** from both primitive urine and urine (not filtered).
  - **Glucose**: present in primitive urine but **absent** from urine (fully reabsorbed).
  - **Urea**: much **more concentrated** in urine than in primitive urine (water reabsorbed, urea not).
- **Liver (肝臓)** functions: converts toxic **ammonia → urea (尿素)** (urea cycle); stores **glycogen** and regulates blood glucose; **detoxifies**; makes **bile** and plasma proteins.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Concentration ratio** $=\dfrac{\text{urine concentration}}{\text{primitive-urine concentration}}$; a high ratio (e.g. urea) means water was reabsorbed but that substance was not.
- **Glucose in urine = 0** normally (fully reabsorbed); its presence signals diabetes.
- Protein concentration in primitive urine $\approx 0$ (too large to filter).

## How the EJU tests it
Given primitive-urine and urine concentrations of three components, **identify which is $\mathrm{Na^+}$, glucose, and protein** based on filtration and reabsorption. Or state a liver function.

## Worked example
Component X: in blood but 0 in primitive urine and urine → **protein** (not filtered). Component Y: in primitive urine but 0 in urine → **glucose** (fully reabsorbed). Component Z: present throughout but more concentrated in urine → an ion like $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (partly reabsorbed).

## Common mistakes
- Thinking glucose appears in normal urine — it is **fully reabsorbed**.
- Expecting protein in primitive urine — it is **too large to be filtered**.
- Attributing urea production to the kidney — the **liver** makes urea; the kidney excretes it.
endocrine-bloodsugar:
**Hormones from endocrine glands regulate the body slowly; blood glucose is held steady by antagonistic hormones — insulin lowers it, while glucagon and adrenaline raise it.**

## Overview
The **endocrine system** controls the body with **hormones** — chemical messengers carried in the blood to target organs. Its showcase example is **blood-sugar regulation**, a negative-feedback loop using opposing hormones. The EJU tests **matching gland → hormone → effect** and labeling a **blood-glucose control diagram** with the correct nerves and hormones.

## Key concepts
- **Hormone (ホルモン)**: made by an **endocrine gland**, released into the blood, and acting on distant **target cells**. Slow to start but long-lasting (vs fast, brief nerve signals).
- **Pancreas (すい臓) — Islets of Langerhans (ランゲルハンス島)**: contain **B (β) cells** that secrete **insulin (インスリン)** and **A (α) cells** that secrete **glucagon (グルカゴン)**.
- **When blood glucose (血糖) is HIGH**: sensed by the pancreas / **hypothalamus (視床下部)** → **insulin** released → body cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as **glycogen** → blood sugar **falls**. Insulin is the only sugar-lowering hormone.
- **When blood glucose is LOW**: → **glucagon** (from pancreas) and **adrenaline (アドレナリン)** (from the adrenal medulla) released → liver breaks glycogen down to glucose → blood sugar **rises**. Glucocorticoids (adrenal cortex) also raise it.
- This is **negative feedback with antagonistic hormones**. The **hypothalamus** and **autonomic nerves** (sympathetic raises sugar, parasympathetic promotes insulin) coordinate it.
- **Diabetes**: insulin lacking or ineffective → blood sugar stays high → glucose appears in urine.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Insulin ↓ blood glucose; glucagon and adrenaline ↑ blood glucose.**
- Glycogen ⇌ glucose: insulin drives storage (glucose → glycogen); glucagon/adrenaline drive release (glycogen → glucose).
- The pancreas islets have **B cells → insulin**, **A cells → glucagon**.

## How the EJU tests it
Label a **blood-glucose regulation diagram**: name the **autonomic nerves** ($\rm I$–$\rm III$: sympathetic/parasympathetic) and **hormones** ($X$–$Z$: insulin, glucagon, adrenaline). Or a true/false statement on which hormone does what.

## Worked example
"Blood sugar has risen after a meal — which hormone restores it and how?" → **insulin** from pancreatic B cells; it makes cells absorb glucose and the liver store glycogen, lowering blood sugar.

## Common mistakes
- Reversing insulin and glucagon — **insulin lowers**, glucagon raises.
- Forgetting that **several** hormones raise blood sugar but only **one** (insulin) lowers it.
- Confusing endocrine (blood-borne, slow) with nervous (fast) control.
autonomic-thermoregulation:
**The autonomic nervous system controls organs involuntarily through antagonistic sympathetic ('fight-or-flight') and parasympathetic ('rest-and-digest') nerves; the hypothalamus is the thermostat that adjusts heat production and loss.**

## Overview
Many body functions run without conscious control via the **autonomic nervous system**, whose two branches have **opposite** effects on each organ. A key application is **thermoregulation** — holding body temperature constant, coordinated by the **hypothalamus**. The EJU tests **sympathetic vs parasympathetic effects** and the responses to a temperature change (often "choose the false statement").

## Key concepts
- **Sympathetic nerve (交感神経)** — "fight or flight": speeds up the **heartbeat**, dilates pupils, raises blood sugar, inhibits digestion. Active in stress/activity.
- **Parasympathetic nerve (副交感神経)** — "rest and digest": **slows the heartbeat**, constricts pupils, promotes digestion. Active at rest.
- They are **antagonistic** — opposite effects on the same organ (e.g. heart: sympathetic accelerates, parasympathetic slows).
- **Heartbeat regulation**: the sinoatrial node's rate is tuned by these nerves.
- **Thermoregulation (体温調節)** — the **hypothalamus** is the control center:
  - **When cold**: shiver (muscle heat), **constrict skin blood vessels** (less heat loss), raise metabolism (thyroxine, adrenaline), **erect hairs** via the **arrector pili (立毛筋)**. Sweating stops.
  - **When hot**: **sweat** (evaporative cooling), **dilate skin blood vessels** (more heat loss), lower metabolism.
- This is negative feedback: the hypothalamus detects deviation and triggers the reversing response.

## Formulas & key facts
- Sympathetic ↑ heart rate; parasympathetic ↓ heart rate (antagonistic).
- Cold response = **increase heat production + decrease heat loss** (constrict vessels, shiver, arrector pili raise hair).
- Hot response = **increase heat loss** (sweat, dilate vessels).

## How the EJU tests it
Choose the **true pair** of autonomic-nerve effects on an organ, or the **false statement** about the body's response to a temperature drop (e.g. "skin blood vessels dilate" is false when cold — they constrict). Watch the direction carefully.

## Worked example
"On body-temperature drop, which is INCORRECT?" — if an option says "skin arterioles dilate," it is **false**; when cold, vessels **constrict** to conserve heat.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing up which branch speeds vs slows the heart (sympathetic **speeds**, parasympathetic **slows**).
- On cooling, wrongly saying vessels dilate — they **constrict** to retain heat.
- Forgetting the **hypothalamus** is the thermoregulation center.
immunity:
**Immunity defends the body: non-specific innate defenses act fast, while specific adaptive immunity (antibodies from B cells, T cells) provides memory, giving a faster, larger secondary response — the basis of vaccines.**

## Overview
The immune system distinguishes self from non-self and destroys pathogens. It has a fast **non-specific** layer and a slower **specific (adaptive)** layer that "remembers" past invaders. The EJU tests the roles of **B and T cells**, the **primary vs secondary response** (an antibody-titer graph), and applications like **vaccines**, **serotherapy**, and **HIV/AIDS**.

## Key concepts
- **Innate (non-specific) immunity**: skin barriers, and **phagocytes** (macrophages, neutrophils) that engulf invaders; fast, no memory.
- **Adaptive (specific) immunity** — lymphocytes recognize a specific **antigen (抗原)**:
  - **B cells** become plasma cells that make **antibodies (抗体)** — humoral immunity. An antibody binds its specific antigen (antigen–antibody reaction).
  - **Helper T cells (ヘルパーT細胞)** activate B cells and killer T cells (they coordinate the response).
  - **Killer (cytotoxic) T cells (キラーT細胞)** destroy virus-infected cells — cell-mediated immunity.
- **Immunological memory**: after a first exposure, **memory cells** remain. A **second exposure** triggers a **secondary response (二次応答)** — antibodies appear **faster and in far larger amounts** than the primary response.
- **Vaccine (ワクチン)**: a harmless form of an antigen given to create memory cells, so a real infection meets a strong secondary response (**active** immunity).
- **Serotherapy (血清療法)**: injecting ready-made **antibodies** (serum) for immediate but temporary protection (**passive** immunity), e.g. against snake venom.
- **HIV/AIDS**: HIV infects and destroys **helper T cells**, crippling the whole adaptive response → immune deficiency.

## Formulas & key facts
- **Secondary response** = faster onset + higher antibody level than the primary — the key graph feature.
- Antibodies come from **B cells** (plasma cells); helper T cells **activate** but do not make antibodies.
- Vaccine → **active** (memory-based) immunity; serotherapy → **passive** (borrowed antibodies) immunity.

## How the EJU tests it
Interpret an **antibody-titer graph**: choose the curve where the **second** injection gives a faster, larger antibody rise (secondary response). Or choose the correct statement about immunity (vaccine, serotherapy, HIV infecting helper T cells, self/non-self).

## Worked example
On an antibody-amount vs time graph, after the 1st antigen dose antibodies rise slowly and low; after the 2nd dose (same antigen) they rise **quickly and much higher** — that steeper, larger second peak is the **secondary response**.

## Common mistakes
- Saying antibodies come from **T cells** — they come from **B cells**.
- Confusing **vaccine** (active, makes your own memory) with **serotherapy** (passive, injected antibodies).
- Forgetting HIV targets **helper T cells** specifically.
nervous-sensory-muscle:
**The nervous system senses stimuli, processes them, and drives movement through muscle — signals are electrical inside neurons and chemical at synapses.**

## Overview
This topic covers how animals detect changes (senses), transmit and integrate information (neurons and brain), and produce movement (muscle). The logic is a single pathway: **receptor → sensory neuron → central nervous system (CNS) → motor neuron → effector**. The EJU treats each stage as a separate item — an action-potential graph, a brain-region function, an eye/ear diagram, or the ordered steps of muscle contraction — so you must know the mechanism at each stage, not just names.

## Key concepts
- **Neuron (ニューロン)**: the signalling cell. Inside one neuron the signal is **electrical** (an **action potential**); between neurons at a **synapse** it is **chemical** (neurotransmitter), so it flows **one way only**.
- **All-or-none**: a neuron fires a full-size action potential once the stimulus passes **threshold (閾値)**, or not at all. A stronger stimulus raises firing *frequency*, never spike *size*.
- **Reflex (反射)**: a fast, automatic response routed through the spinal cord (**reflex arc, 反射弓**) without waiting for the brain.
- **Brain regions**: **cerebrum (大脳)** = thought, memory, voluntary movement; **cerebellum (小脳)** = balance and coordinated movement; **medulla oblongata (延髄)** = breathing, heartbeat, reflexes; **midbrain (中脳)** = eye/posture reflexes.
- **Senses**: the **eye** detects light (retina with rods and cones); the **ear** detects sound (cochlea) and rotation/tilt (semicircular canals).
- **Muscle**: converts ATP chemical energy into movement by the **sliding-filament** mechanism, triggered by $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.

## Formulas & key facts
- Resting potential $\approx -70\ \mathrm{mV}$ (inside negative), maintained by the $\mathrm{Na^+/K^+}$ pump.
- Depolarisation = $\mathrm{Na^+}$ inflow; repolarisation = $\mathrm{K^+}$ outflow.
- Reflex-arc order: **receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay) → motor neuron → effector**.

## How the EJU tests it
Expect single-best-answer MCQs: choose the graph of **action potential vs stimulus strength** (all-or-none), name the **brain region** responsible for a function, order the **cochlea/muscle steps**, or pick the true/false statement about a sense organ. Terms are glossed bilingually (Japanese with English in parentheses).

## Common mistakes
- Thinking a bigger stimulus gives a bigger spike — it changes frequency, not amplitude.
- Confusing cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla functions.
- Forgetting synaptic transmission is one-directional (chemical), while conduction within an axon is electrical and bidirectional in principle.
neuron-brain:
**A neuron transmits an all-or-none electrical action potential; the brain and spinal cord integrate these signals, and reflexes take a fast shortcut through the spinal cord.**

## Overview
A **neuron (ニューロン)** carries information as brief electrical pulses. Understanding the exam item means understanding three things: how the resting cell is charged, how an **action potential (活動電位)** is generated and why it obeys the **all-or-none** rule, and how signals are routed through the brain and through **reflex arcs (反射弓)**. This is one of the most reliably tested biology topics.

## Key concepts
- **Resting potential**: at rest the inside of the axon is negative ($\approx -70\ \mathrm{mV}$). The $\mathrm{Na^+/K^+}$ pump keeps $\mathrm{Na^+}$ high outside and $\mathrm{K^+}$ high inside.
- **Action potential (活動電位)**: a stimulus above **threshold (閾値)** opens $\mathrm{Na^+}$ channels → $\mathrm{Na^+}$ rushes in → the membrane **depolarises** (briefly positive inside). Then $\mathrm{K^+}$ channels open → $\mathrm{K^+}$ flows out → **repolarisation** back to rest.
- **All-or-none**: a single neuron either fires a full-size spike or nothing. A **stronger stimulus** does NOT enlarge the spike — it increases the **frequency** of spikes and recruits more neurons.
- **Conduction speed**: faster in **myelinated** axons (saltatory conduction, jumping node to node) and in **thicker** axons.
- **Synapse**: the impulse triggers **neurotransmitter** release; it diffuses across the gap and binds receptors on the next cell. Because only one side releases transmitter, transmission is **one-directional**.
- **Reflex arc (反射弓)**: **receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector**. The knee-jerk and withdrawal reflexes bypass the brain, so they are fast; you become *aware* only afterwards.
- **Brain regions**: **cerebrum (大脳)** — thought, memory, sensation, voluntary movement; **cerebellum (小脳)** — balance and smooth coordinated movement; **medulla oblongata (延髄)** — breathing, heartbeat, swallowing, vomiting; **midbrain (中脳)** — pupil and posture reflexes; **diencephalon** (hypothalamus) — homeostasis. Cerebrum + cerebellum + brainstem structures are the standard set to distinguish.

## Formulas & key facts
- $V_{\text{rest}} \approx -70\ \mathrm{mV}$; depolarisation driven by $\mathrm{Na^+}$ in, repolarisation by $\mathrm{K^+}$ out.
- Spike amplitude is constant (all-or-none); information is coded by **frequency**.

## How the EJU tests it
- Choose the graph of **spike size (or frequency) vs stimulus strength** — the correct answer keeps amplitude flat once threshold is passed (all-or-none). (cf. 2020_2 Q14.)
- Identify the brain region for a stated function, e.g. **balance → cerebellum** (cf. 2019_1 Q12), or the reflex centre (spinal cord/medulla).
- Order the reflex-arc components, or pick the correct statement about synaptic (one-way) transmission.

## Worked example
A researcher applies increasing stimulus strength to one sensory neuron and records the action potentials. Once the stimulus exceeds threshold, each spike has the **same height**; further increases make spikes occur **more often**. Correct answer: "spike size stays constant, frequency increases" — the all-or-none principle.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming a stronger stimulus makes a taller action potential in a single neuron — it does not.
- Swapping cerebellum (balance/coordination) with cerebrum (thought) or medulla (heartbeat/breathing).
- Thinking a reflex "goes to the brain first" — the reflex arc acts through the spinal cord before conscious awareness.
- Forgetting that synaptic transmission is chemical and one-way.
sensory-organs:
**The eye converts light into nerve signals at the retina (rods for dim light, cones for colour); the ear detects sound in the cochlea and detects rotation/tilt in the semicircular canals.**

## Overview
Sensory organs turn a physical stimulus into an action potential. The EJU focuses on two: the **eye** (light → retina) and the **ear** (sound → cochlea; balance → semicircular canals). You must know the **path** the stimulus takes, which cells respond to what, and how pitch and rotation are detected. Items are usually diagram-based.

## Key concepts
- **Eye light path**: light → cornea → pupil (iris adjusts diameter) → lens (focuses) → **retina (網膜)** at the back. The retina's receptor cells face *away* from the incoming light, so light passes through inner layers before reaching the receptors.
- **Rod cells (桿体細胞)**: very sensitive, work in **dim light**, give **no colour**; contain the pigment rhodopsin. Abundant in the periphery.
- **Cone cells (錐体細胞)**: work in **bright light**, detect **colour** (three types), give sharp vision. Concentrated at the **fovea** (中心窩), the point of sharpest sight.
- **Blind spot**: where the optic nerve exits — no receptor cells, so no image forms there.
- **Accommodation**: the ciliary muscle changes lens thickness — **thicker lens for near** objects, thinner for far.
- **Ear — hearing**: sound → eardrum → three ossicles (amplify) → **cochlea (うずまき管)**, a coiled fluid-filled tube. Hair cells on the basilar membrane bend and fire.
- **Frequency (pitch) reception**: different positions along the cochlea respond to different frequencies — the base (near the entrance) responds to **high** frequencies, the apex (far end) to **low** frequencies. This place-coding is a favourite EJU point.
- **Semicircular canals (半規管)**: three loops at right angles; fluid movement bends hair cells to sense **rotation**. The nearby vestibule (otolith organs) senses **tilt/gravity (回転・傾き)** and linear acceleration.

## Formulas & key facts
- Rods: dim light, no colour, high sensitivity. Cones: bright light, colour, high acuity (fovea).
- Cochlea place-coding: high pitch near base, low pitch at apex.
- Balance: semicircular canals → rotation; vestibule/otolith → tilt and gravity.

## How the EJU tests it
- Label retina layers and indicate the **direction light travels** and where rods/cones sit (cf. 2018_2 Q12).
- Order **pitch reception along the cochlea** and identify the fluids/regions (cf. 2021_1 Q12).
- Choose the correct statement matching a structure to its function (rods vs cones; canals vs cochlea). Single-best-answer MCQ, terms glossed bilingually.

## Worked example
"Which cells let you see colour in a brightly lit room, and where are they densest?" → **Cone cells (錐体細胞)**, densest at the **fovea**. In near-darkness you rely on **rod cells**, which give no colour — this is why colours fade at night.

## Common mistakes
- Swapping rods and cones (rods = dim/no colour; cones = colour/bright).
- Assigning hearing to the semicircular canals — hearing is the **cochlea**; canals sense rotation/balance.
- Thinking the lens gets thinner for near objects — it gets **thicker** for near vision.
- Forgetting the retina's receptors face away from the light.
muscle-contraction:
**Muscle shortens by the sliding-filament mechanism: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum exposes actin binding sites so myosin heads pull the actin filaments inward, powered by ATP.**

## Overview
Skeletal muscle is built from repeating units called **sarcomeres (サルコメア)** containing thin **actin (アクチン)** and thick **myosin (ミオシン)** filaments. Contraction is not the filaments getting shorter — they **slide past each other** so the sarcomere shortens. The EJU tests the **ordered trigger sequence** ($\mathrm{Ca^{2+}} \to$ troponin $\to$ tropomyosin $\to$ actin–myosin) and which sarcomere bands change on contraction.

## Key concepts
- **Sarcomere (サルコメア)**: the contractile unit between two Z-lines. Thin filaments (**actin**) anchor at the Z-lines; thick filaments (**myosin**) sit in the middle.
- **Regulatory proteins on actin**: **tropomyosin (トロポミオシン)** is a strand that, at rest, **blocks** the myosin-binding sites on actin. **Troponin (トロポニン)** binds $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and, when it does, moves tropomyosin aside, **unblocking** the sites.
- **Sarcoplasmic reticulum (筋小胞体)**: an internal store of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$. A nerve impulse causes it to **release $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$** into the cytoplasm; when signalling stops, it pumps $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ back and the muscle relaxes.
- **Sliding-filament mechanism (滑り説)**: with sites exposed, **myosin heads bind actin, pivot (power stroke), and pull actin toward the sarcomere centre**. ATP binds the myosin head to release it, then is hydrolysed to re-cock the head for the next cycle. Repeated cycling = contraction.
- **Band changes on contraction**: the sarcomere and the **I-band** (actin-only) and **H-zone** (myosin-only) **shorten**; the **A-band** (= length of the myosin filament) stays **constant** because the filaments themselves do not change length.

## Formulas & key facts
- Trigger order: **nerve impulse → $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum → $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ binds troponin → tropomyosin shifts → actin sites exposed → myosin binds & pulls (ATP-powered) → sarcomere shortens**.
- On contraction: I-band ↓, H-zone ↓, **A-band unchanged**; Z-lines move closer.
- ATP is needed both to power the power stroke *and* to detach myosin from actin (why muscles stiffen without ATP).

## How the EJU tests it
- **Order the contraction steps** into the correct sequence (cf. 2021_1 Q13).
- Choose the correct/incorrect **muscle statement** — commonly about which band changes, or the role of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and ATP (cf. 2018_2 Q13).
- Interpret a sarcomere diagram before vs after contraction. Single-best-answer MCQ.

## Worked example
"During contraction, which region does NOT change length?" → the **A-band**, because it equals the myosin filament length, and myosin does not shorten. The I-band and H-zone shrink as actin slides inward. Meanwhile $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}} \to$ troponin frees the actin sites; this is the correct causal order.

## Common mistakes
- Saying the filaments shorten — they **slide**; only the sarcomere shortens.
- Reversing the trigger order (troponin binds $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ *before* tropomyosin moves).
- Claiming the A-band shrinks — it stays constant; the I-band and H-zone shrink.
- Forgetting ATP is needed to **detach** myosin, not only to power the stroke.
plant-physiology:
**Plants respond to their environment through hormones and directional growth, and time their flowering by night length; animals respond through innate and learned behaviour.**

## Overview
This topic groups plant physiology (hormones, tropisms, germination, flowering) with animal behaviour (innate vs learned). The unifying theme is **response to environmental cues** — light, gravity, day length, and experience. On the EJU each subtopic appears as its own item: a coleoptile phototropism experiment, a germination hormone blank-fill, a flowering light/dark regime, or a "classify this behaviour" question.

## Key concepts
- **Plant hormones**: **auxin (オーキシン)** drives cell elongation and phototropism; **gibberellin (ジベレリン)** promotes germination and stem growth; **abscisic acid (アブシシン酸)** promotes dormancy and closes stomata. Plants do not have muscle — "movement" is directional **growth (tropism)** from uneven hormone distribution.
- **Photoperiodism**: flowering is controlled by the length of **continuous darkness**, not day length directly. **Long-day plants (長日植物)** flower when nights are short; **short-day plants (短日植物)** flower when nights are long.
- **Animal behaviour**: **innate behaviour (生得的行動)** is inborn (taxis, fixed action patterns, reflexes); **learning (学習)** is modified by experience (habituation, imprinting, conditioning).

## Formulas & key facts
- Auxin accumulates on the **shaded** side of a shoot → that side elongates more → shoot bends **toward** light.
- Flowering depends on **critical dark period (限界暗期)**; a night-break (light flash) resets it.
- Innate = no experience needed; learned = requires experience.

## How the EJU tests it
Single-best-answer MCQs: blank-fill on germination hormones (gibberellin promotes, abscisic acid inhibits, amylase digests starch); interpret coleoptile experiments (mica/gelatin inserts) for auxin movement; predict flowering from light/dark diagrams; classify a behaviour as innate or learned. Terms are glossed bilingually.

## Common mistakes
- Saying day length (not night length) controls flowering — it is the **uninterrupted dark period**.
- Thinking auxin gathers on the lit side — it gathers on the **shaded** side.
- Confusing habituation (learned) with a simple reflex (innate).
plant-hormones:
**Plant hormones control growth and development: auxin drives cell elongation and phototropism, gibberellin promotes germination and stem growth, and abscisic acid enforces dormancy.**

## Overview
Plants coordinate growth chemically. The EJU concentrates on three hormones — **auxin (オーキシン)**, **gibberellin (ジベレリン)**, **abscisic acid (アブシシン酸)** — plus the classic **coleoptile (幼葉鞘)** phototropism experiments and the hormonal control of **germination (発芽)**. You must reason through experiment diagrams (where light comes from, where inserts block auxin) rather than just recall facts.

## Key concepts
- **Auxin (オーキシン)** = indoleacetic acid (**IAA, インドール酢酸**): made at the **shoot tip**, it moves **downward** (and only downward — polar transport) and **promotes cell elongation**.
- **Phototropism (光屈性)**: light causes auxin to move to the **shaded side** of the coleoptile. The shaded side, with more auxin, elongates faster, so the shoot **bends toward the light**. The tip is where light is sensed; elongation occurs just below the tip.
- **Opposite root/shoot sensitivity**: the same auxin concentration that **promotes** shoot growth **inhibits** roots. So in gravitropism, auxin collects on the lower side: shoots bend **up** (that side elongates), roots bend **down** (that side is inhibited).
- **Coleoptile (幼葉鞘)** experiments: an opaque cap or a **mica** (impermeable) insert blocks bending; a permeable **gelatin/agar** block lets auxin pass, so bending still occurs. These distinguish "is auxin a chemical that can diffuse?" (yes).
- **Gibberellin (ジベレリン)**: promotes **stem elongation** and, crucially, **germination**. In a seed, the embryo secretes gibberellin, which triggers cells to produce **amylase (アミラーゼ)**; amylase digests stored starch into sugar to fuel the sprouting embryo.
- **Abscisic acid (アブシシン酸)**: the antagonist — promotes seed **dormancy**, **inhibits germination**, and closes stomata under water stress.

## Formulas & key facts
- Auxin: shoot tip → moves down → elongation; concentrates on shaded/lower side.
- Germination: **gibberellin → amylase → starch broken to sugar**; **abscisic acid inhibits** germination.
- Root vs shoot: identical auxin dose promotes shoots but inhibits roots (dose–response curves differ).

## How the EJU tests it
- **Germination blank-fill**: fill in gibberellin (promotes), amylase, and abscisic acid (inhibits) — cf. 2021_1 Q14.
- **Coleoptile phototropism**: deduce auxin movement/bending from mica vs gelatin inserts and light direction (cf. 2019_1 Q15).
- **Auxin concentration–response** table/graph: read which concentration best promotes shoots vs roots (cf. 2018_2 Q14). Single-best-answer MCQ.

## Worked example
A coleoptile is lit from the left. Auxin from the tip moves to the **right (shaded) side**; the right side elongates faster, so the shoot **curves toward the left light**. If a **mica** sheet is inserted to block lateral auxin flow, no bending occurs; if a permeable **agar** block replaces the tip, bending resumes — showing auxin is a diffusible chemical.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking auxin gathers on the **lit** side — it moves to the **shaded** side.
